name: Keema Matar
subtitle: minced mutton browned hard with peas, the sunday lunch of a punjabi kitchen

ingredients.note: goat mince with some fat; lean mince goes dry

prepNotes: Take the mince out of the fridge 20 minutes before cooking so it browns instead of steaming.
Chop the onions fine and evenly. This masala is bhuna-ed hard and uneven pieces burn before the rest colours.
If using frozen peas, thaw and drain them; add them only in the last 8 minutes or they turn grey.

steps.text: Heat the ghee in a pressure cooker, crackle the cumin, then add the bay, black cardamom, cinnamon and cloves for 20 seconds.
Add the onion and cook on medium for 12-14 minutes to a deep even gold, stirring often.
steps.tip: This is where the colour of the finished keema comes from. Pale onion, pale keema.

steps.text: Stir in the ginger and garlic pastes and the green chillies and fry 2 minutes, until the raw smell goes.
Add the turmeric, chilli powder, coriander and cumin powders with a splash of water and cook 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes and salt and cook 8-10 minutes until they collapse and the ghee separates at the edge of the pan.
Turn the heat high, add the mince and break it up constantly for 8 minutes until no pink remains and the grains are separate and browned.
steps.tip: Do not add water or cover it here. The mince must fry, not stew, or the keema tastes flat.

steps.text: Lower the heat, beat in the whisked yogurt a spoon at a time, and fry 3 minutes more.
Add 250ml water, close the cooker and cook 3 whistles, then 10 minutes on low. Rest until the pressure drops.
Open, stir in the peas and simmer uncovered 8 minutes, until the peas are tender and the keema is moist but not soupy.
steps.tip: Cook off any loose liquid at this stage — keema matar should hold its shape on a spoon.

steps.text: Crush in the kasuri methi, add the garam masala, cover and rest 5 minutes off the heat. Finish with coriander leaves.

storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and freezes well for 2 months. Reheat in a pan with 2-3 tbsp water over low heat; the fat will re-emulsify as it warms.
